### C.

#### Kits

```{r}
genes<-read.csv("https://calvin-data304.netlify.app/data/twins-genetics-long.csv")
str(genes)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: TRUE

vl_chart(height = 400, width = 600) |>
  vl_mark_bar() |>
  vl_encode_x("pair:N", title = "Twin Pair ID #") |>
  vl_encode_y("genetic.share:Q", title = "Genetic Share") |>
  vl_encode_color("kit:N", scale = list(scheme = "category10")) |>
  vl_facet_column("id:N",title = "Genetic Share Across Twin Pairs by Kit") |>
  vl_encode_xOffset("kit")|>
  vl_add_data(genes)


```

This bar graph highlights that, although twins tend to share nearly all their DNA, small variations do occur. By creating a side-by-side bar graph, it's easier for the human eye to compare these variations. I hope that this graphic can help explain differences between twins, such as their appearance and health.

```{r}
#| code-fold: TRUE

vl_chart(height = 500, width = 700, title = "Genetic Similarity Across DNA Test Kits") |>
  vl_mark_rect()|>  
  vl_encode_x("kit:N", title = "DNA Test Kit") |>
  vl_encode_y("pair:N", title = "Twin Pair") |>
  vl_encode_color("genetic.share:Q", scale = list(scheme = "dark2"), title = "Genetic Share") |>  
  vl_add_data(genes)


```

This heat map shows the differences in how various DNA test kits report genetic similarity for each twin pair. The color palette represents the reported genetic share, with darker colors indicating lower similarity and lighter colors indicating higher similarity. This graphic highlights the potential inconsistency of the DNA testing kits.

## Exercise 2 (Data and graphics challenge)

![Analysis](AnalysisForPortfolio.png)

-   How our business compares to other businesses (over time and in February 2020):

    -   Business's Net Promoter Score (NPS) compared to other businesses over time, showing trends from January 2019 to February 2020. This analysis allows us to see how business's NPS has evolved compared to the competition. By examining these trends, we can identify periods where the business performed well and pinpoint times that may have had challenges. In February 2020 specifically, we can see NPS in relation to competitors, providing a snapshot of the market position at that time.

-   How the components of the net promoter score for our business have changed over time:

    -   The NPS components for the business (Detractors, Passives, Promoters) have changed from January 2019 to February 2020. By analyzing these changes, we gain insights into customer sentiment. For example, an increase in Promoters indicates higher customer satisfaction and loyalty, while an increase in Detractors suggests areas that need improvement. This breakdown helps us understand how the composition of the NPS score has evolved.

## Exercise 3 (A new challenge)

```{r}
tanzania<-read.csv("tanzaniaDataSet.csv")
str(tanzania)
```

### Data wrangling

```{r}
# Renaming the variables
tanzania_clean <- tanzania |>
  rename(
    Survey_Year = DHS.Survey.Year,
    Total_fertility_Rate = Total.Fertility.Rate..ages.15.49.,
    Contraception_Rate = Contraception....,
    Unmet_Planning_Rate = Unmet.Planning....
  )
# Dealing with the years
tanzania_split <- tanzania_clean |>
 separate(Survey_Year, into = c("start_year", "end_year"), sep = "-", fill = "right") |>
  # Convert to integers
  mutate(
    start_year = as.integer(start_year),
    end_year = ifelse(is.na(end_year), start_year, as.integer(end_year))
  ) |>
  # Replicate data for each year in the range
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(year = list(seq(start_year, end_year))) |>
  unnest(cols = c(year)) |>
  select(-start_year, -end_year)

#Arrage by year ascending
sorted_tanzania_split <- tanzania_split |>
  arrange(year)
#converting to long
sorted_tanzania_split_long <- sorted_tanzania_split |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Total_fertility_Rate, Contraception_Rate, Unmet_Planning_Rate),
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")
#converting to appropriate type
sorted_tanzania_split_long$variable <- factor(sorted_tanzania_split_long$variable)

sorted_tanzania_split_long$year <- as.numeric(sorted_tanzania_split_long$year)

sorted_tanzania_split_long$year <- as.numeric(as.character(sorted_tanzania_split_long$year))

sorted_tanzania_split_long$variable <- gsub("_", " ", sorted_tanzania_split_long$variable)
str(sorted_tanzania_split_long)

sorted_tanzania_split_long <- sorted_tanzania_split_long |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(proportion = value / sum(value)) |>
  ungroup()
```

### Graphic

```{r}
#| code-fold: TRUE

#EDA
sorted_tanzania_split_long <- as.data.frame(sorted_tanzania_split_long)

line_chart <- vl_chart(height = 400, width = 600) |>
  vl_mark_line(point = TRUE) |>
  vl_encode_x("year", type = "ordinal", axis = list(labelAngle = 0), title = "") |>
  vl_encode_y("value", type = "quantitative", title = "Rate (%)") |>
  vl_add_data(sorted_tanzania_split_long) 

line_chart <-line_chart |>
  vl_encode_color("variable", type = "nominal", title = "Variable") |>
  vl_add_point_selection("variable_param", bind = "legend", encodings = list("color") )|>
  vl_encode_opacity(value = 0.2) |>
  vl_condition_opacity(param = "variable_param", value = 1)

line_chart


bar_chart <- vl_chart(height = 400, width = 600) |>
  vl_mark_bar() |>
  vl_encode_x("year", type = "ordinal", axis = list(labelAngle = 0), title = "") |>
  vl_encode_y("proportion", type = "quantitative", title = "Proportion") |>
  vl_add_data(sorted_tanzania_split_long) |>
  vl_encode_color("variable", type = "nominal", title = "Variable")
bar_chart





combined_chart <- vl_concat(
  line_chart,
  bar_chart,
 columns = 2
)

combined_chart

```

The story I am trying to tell with the graphic above is a simple one: how the different rates of patterns of reproductive health have evolved in Tanzania. For example, the fertility rate has dropped slightly since the first survey, while the contraception rate has increased almost exponentially, with the data plateauing in the last two years, which is the last survey.

## Exercise 4 (Your masterpiece)

```{r}
strokeData <- read.csv("strokeData.csv")
str(strokeData)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: TRUE

# EDA
strokeData$Age <- as.integer(strokeData$Age)
  
strokeData_select <- strokeData |>
  select(Age, BMI, Avg_Glucose, Stroke)  

interactive_plot <- vl_chart(height = 400, width = 600) |>
  vl_mark_circle() |>
  vl_encode_x("Age", type = "quantitative", title = "Age") |>  
  vl_encode_y("BMI", type = "quantitative", title = "BMI") |>
  vl_encode_tooltip_array(c("Avg_Glucose", "BMI", "Age", "Stroke")) |>
  vl_add_data(strokeData_select) |>
  
  vl_add_parameter("Avg_Glucose", value = min(strokeData$Avg_Glucose)) |>
  vl_bind_range_input(
    parameter_name = "Avg_Glucose", 
    name = "Avg Glucose: ",                 
    min = min(strokeData$Avg_Glucose),
    max = max(strokeData$Avg_Glucose)
  ) |>
  vl_filter("datum.Avg_Glucose <= Avg_Glucose") |>
  
    vl_encode_color("Stroke", type = "nominal", title = "Stroke Status") |>
  vl_add_point_selection("variable_param", bind = "legend", encodings = list("color") )|>
  vl_encode_opacity(value = 0.2) |>
  vl_condition_opacity(param = "variable_param", value = 1)
interactive_plot

strokeData_Diabetes <- strokeData |>
  filter(Diabetes == 1)
#Intersting 
threshold_chart <- vl_chart(height = 400, width = 600) |>
  vl_mark_circle() |>
  vl_encode_x("Avg_Glucose", type = "quantitative", title = "Average Glucose Level") |>  
  vl_encode_y("BMI", type = "quantitative", title = "BMI") |>
  vl_encode_color(
    legend = TRUE, condition = list(
      test = "datum.Avg_Glucose > threshold_param",  # Condition for threshold
      value = "red"  # Color for points above the threshold
    ),
    value = "blue"  # Default color
  ) |>
  vl_add_data(strokeData_Diabetes) |>
  
  # Add a parameter for the threshold
  vl_add_parameter("threshold_param", value = 120) |>
  vl_bind_range_input(
    parameter_name = "threshold_param", 
    name = "Glucose Threshold: ",                 
    min = min(strokeData_Diabetes$Avg_Glucose),
    max = max(strokeData_Diabetes$Avg_Glucose)
  )


threshold_chart


```

For the first graphic, I want to show how, as you age, the average glucose level tends to be higher, and the same is true for BMI. In the second graphic, I want to show how much people's glucose levels can exceed the dynamic average glucose level in this dataset, controlled by a slider. Additionally, I added an interactive legend so the user can focus on the group that had a stroke, the group that didn’t, or both at the same time.

```{r}
#| code-fold: TRUE
interactive_plot <- vl_chart(height = 400, width = 600) |>
  vl_mark_boxplot() |>
  vl_encode_x("Smoking_Status", type = "nominal", axis = list(labelAngle = 0), title = "Smoking Status") |>
  vl_encode_y("Avg_Glucose", type = "quantitative", title = "Average Glucose Level") |>
  vl_encode_color("Stroke", type = "nominal", title = "Stroke Status") |>
  vl_encode_tooltip_array(c("Smoking_Status", "Avg_Glucose", "Stroke")) |>
  vl_encode_xOffset("Smoking_Status")|>
  vl_add_data(strokeData)

interactive_plot



```

```{r}
#| code-fold: TRUE

# Convert categorical variables to factors
strokeData <- strokeData |>
  mutate(Gender = as.factor(Gender),
         SES = as.factor(SES),
         Smoking_Status = as.factor(Smoking_Status),
         Hypertension = as.factor(Hypertension),
         Heart_Disease = as.factor(Heart_Disease),
         Diabetes = as.factor(Diabetes),
         Stroke = as.factor(Stroke))  

# Fit Logistic Regression Model
stroke_model <- glm(Stroke ~ Age + Gender + SES + Hypertension + Heart_Disease + 
                     BMI + Avg_Glucose + Diabetes + Smoking_Status, 
                     data = strokeData, family = binomial)

# Predict stroke probabilities
strokeData_select$predicted_prob <- predict(stroke_model, type = "response")

# Create a Vega-Lite visualization
stroke_scatter <- vl_chart(height = 400, width = 600) |>
  vl_mark_circle() |>
  vl_encode_x("Age", type = "quantitative", title = "Age") |>  
  vl_encode_y("predicted_prob", type = "quantitative", title = "Predicted Stroke Probability") |>
  vl_encode_tooltip_array(c("Age", "predicted_prob", "BMI")) |>
  vl_add_data(strokeData_select)
# Fit LOESS model
loess_fit <- loess(predicted_prob ~ Age, data = strokeData_select, span = 0.5)

# Create a new dataset with smoothed values
stroke_loess <- data.frame(
  Age = strokeData_select$Age,
  predicted_smooth = predict(loess_fit, newdata = strokeData_select)
)
# Loess graphic
loess_line <- vl_chart() |> 
  vl_mark_line(color = "red", opacity = 0.8) |>
  vl_encode_x("Age", type = "quantitative") |>  
  vl_encode_y("predicted_smooth", type = "quantitative") |>
  vl_add_data(stroke_loess)

# Layering
final_plot <- vl_layer(stroke_scatter, loess_line)
final_plot

```

I decided to use a basic stroke dataset because, a while back, my dad had five strokes and he had many of the conditions mentioned in the dataset, such as heart disease, hypertension, and he was also a former smoker and currently is a diabetic. At the end of the day it was because he didn’t take care of his diabetes giving him a high average glucose level. The combination of all these factors led and his age ultimately led to his strokes. Which seems to be consistent with the prediction plot.

## Exercise 5 (Using your palette):

a.  an encoding channel other than x or y:

    For most of my graphics, I use other channels of encoding. For example, in the Tanzania graphic, I use encoding for opacity so that when the user selects one of the rates, the other rates become less opaque.

b.  layers:

    In my "masterpiece," I use layers to overlay a scatter plot and a loess line to make the predictions easier to see.

c.  facets:

    In the first twins' graphic, I use a facet to create two different graphics, faceted by the identity of the twins.

d.  concatenation or repeat:

    Again, in the Tanzania example, I use concatenation to show both the trend of rates over time and, on the left, the proportions of the rates per year.

e.  non-default settings for a channel’s scale or guide:

    In the heatmap example, I use a non-default color scale to highlight the differences between the genetic kits.

f.  tooltips:

    I used tooltips in my graphics on "my masterpiece" so that when you hover over a data point, you can observe multiple variables of the dataset for that point.

g.  another kind of interaction (panning/zooming, brushing, sliders, etc.):

    I used a couple of interactions in a few graphs. For example, in the Tanzania line graph, I bound the legend to the opacity so that when the user selects one of the rates on the legend, the other two become less opaque. Another example is in the first graphic of the stroke dataset, where I used a slider for age to observe the data points by age.

## Exercise 6 (Keep learning)

a.  

    -   In the [second graphic](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/docs/condition.html), the stroke dataset ,I added a slider that controls the color based on the threshold, which I set to 120 because that's when it starts to get dangerous for diabetic people. I thought that was interesting because then you can observe who goes beyond that danger zone threshold.

    -   While working on some of my graphics, I saw that the axis were at the wrong angle to the point where trying to read the labels became more important than the actual graphic. So, inorder to remove this, I looked at the documentation for axis and found that you could change the angle of the labels with [labelAngle](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/docs/axis.html). Though it is a small and subtle change, it has an impact on the one observing the graph, shifting the focus from the label to the actual graphic.

b.  

    -   The color for the heat map I chose according to [Wilke](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/color-basics.html#color-as-a-tool-to-distinguish) and the [github page](https://vega.github.io/vega/docs/schemes/) where Wilke advises in section 4.1 to use color as a tool to distinguish and then according to the documentation dark2 is categorical scheme.

    -   For the last stroke graphic, specifically, I followed [Knaflic'](https://github.com/Saurav6789/Books-/blob/master/storytelling-with-data-cole-nussbaumer-knaflic.pdf) advice from chapter 6, page 235. His advice is that visualization without a story doesn't stick with the audience. By adding my father's story about his stroke,s I think I will appeal to the emotion of the audience, and hence,e it will stick with them for longer.
